speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Clause 2 of the Bill seeks to preserve the ease of doing shipping business in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Specifically, this clause exempts Shipowners' Liens from the requirement of registration as a charge under section 131 of the Companies Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A Shipowner's Lien is a standard feature in ship charterparties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A charterparty is a maritime contract, typically between a shipowner and a charterer or a hirer of the shipowner's vessel.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Shipowners' Lien in such a contract gives the shipowner the right, in the event of the charterer's default, to claim payment from monies owing to the charterer by third parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In other words, should the charterer be unable to pay the shipowner, the lien allows the shipowner to directly recover payment of sub-hire, sub-freight or, in certain instances, bill of lading freight, from a sub-charterer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The term "Shipowner's Lien" is the term of the art used by the shipping community to refer to liens provided to others, beyond the registered owner of the ship.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These include a disponent owner, bareboat charterer or other charterer, in addition to the registered owner.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In 2017, the status of an unregistered Shipowner's Lien vis-a-vis a liquidator of the charterer and its interaction with section 131 of the Companies Act was litigated in Singapore for the first time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The High Court in Duncan, Cameron Lindsay v Diablo Fortune Inc recognised a Shipowner's Lien as a charge that is required to be registered under section 131 of the Companies Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In March 2018, the Court of Appeal affirmed the High Court's decision.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As a consequence of non-registration under section 131, the lien in that case was not enforceable against the liquidator of the charterer and the shipowner who would otherwise have had the benefit of the lien, ranked together with the unsecured creditors of the charterer instead.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The effect of the Diablo case gives rise to several practical difficulties for the shipping industry in connection with section 131 of the Companies Act and Shipowners' Liens.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, leaving aside the long-standing industry custom and practice where shipowners do not habitually register Shipowners' Liens, the registration of Shipowners' Liens is particularly difficult from a practical perspective.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is because each ship is typically subject to a continual series of charterparties, each entered into as quickly as possible, to ensure that the ship is continually gainfully employed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Often, charters are for periods as short as a few days.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This means that many charterparties may have been completed before a charge can even be registered.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, given the volume of charterparties, there would likely be significant administrative and cost implications for shipping companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As a result, compliance with section 131 of the Companies Act in relation to Shipowners' Liens would be particularly burdensome for the shipping industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Furthermore, the underlying rationale of section 131 of the Companies Act, which is to protect third parties who deal with companies, by disclosing charges against a company’s property, is less applicable in the shipping context.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As observed by the Court of Appeal in its grounds of decision in the Diablo case, " otice…may not be necessary in the   context since all parties who deal with charterers are aware that such liens are standard in charterparties".

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Moving to the specifics of the amendment, there is precedent for the introduction of a statutory exemption from registration under section 131 of the Companies Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, section 131(3A) of the Companies Act exempts charges over securities issued by the Government.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There is international precedent for excluding Shipowners' Liens from registration requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In Hong Kong, for example, the Hong Kong Companies Ordinance stipulates that a Shipowners' Lien does not amount to a charge and, consequently, Shipowners' Liens are excluded from the requirement of registration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In our case, the Bill, while exempting such Shipowners' Liens from registration requirements under section 131 of the Companies Act, maintains the Singapore Courts' characterisation in the Diablo case of such liens as charges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The effect of this is that the Shipowners' Lien retains its essential nature as a security but without the need for registration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As a result, the Shipowners' Lien will take priority over other charges created subsequent to it, as well as over unsecured creditors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is unlike Hong Kong where, given that a Shipowners' Lien is not a charge to begin with, it will not take priority over other charges and will rank pari passu with unsecured claims.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, this will be the position for all Shipowners' Liens that are created on or after the date that the amendments in this Bill come into effect.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With regard to Shipowners' Liens that are already in existence, or which are created before the effective date of these amendments, the position is as follows.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Specifically, such unregistered Shipowners’ Liens would generally remain valid, unless the relevant company is already in winding up, or a creditor has already obtained proprietary rights or interests in the subject matter of the charge.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Clause 3 of the Bill seeks to clarify the categories of persons bound by a compromise or scheme of arrangement when a company is in the course of being wound up.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Section 210 of the Companies Act provides the mechanism for a compromise or arrangement to rearrange the rights of the company, its creditors or members.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under the proposed amendments, a shipowner includes a registered owner, a disponent owner or a bareboat charterer of a ship.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Simply put, the shipowner can intercept income due to charterers in the form of bill of lading freight, sub-freight under a voyage charter or sub-hire under a sub-charter.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today's Bill for the proposed amendment of section 131 of the Companies Act stems from the recent Court of Appeal case of Diablo Fortune v Duncan Lindsay.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Court of Appeal, with five judges hearing the appeal, affirmed the decision of Judicial Commissioner Audrey Lim in the High Court below.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Diablo Fortune Inc are the owners of the cargo vessel V8 Stealth II.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Their bareboat chartered the vessel to Siva Ships International Pte Ltd.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The charterers entered into a pooling agreement with another company by which the charterers earned charterhire.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The charterers then went into liquidation and the owners sought to enforce a lien over subhire pursuant to clause 18 of the bareboat charterparty by serving a lien on the pool.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The pool withheld hire payments to the charterer.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The liquidators applied to the High Court directing payment of the charterhire to the charterer.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the High Court decision below, the hon Judicial Commissioner held that the lien over sub-hire created by a charterparty was registrable pursuant to section 131(3)(f) of the Companies Act as a book debt or pursuant to section 131(g) as a floating charge.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The decision in July 2017 last year generated a strong reaction from the maritime community in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Although it can be said that the decisions of the Court of Appeal and the High Court are not surprising given that they are, in some respects, consistent with English law on the registrability of liens on sub-hire and sub-freights, the recent decisions are nonetheless the first local judicial pronouncements on the effect of the non-registration of such liens.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The shipping community, led by the Singapore Shipping Association, bemoaned the “onerous” and “administrative burden” of having to register all such liens and pleaded for a “statutory carve out”.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reaction from the shipping community is perhaps hardly surprising, at least to those in the community.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such a lien clause is very common in standard charterparties all over the world, not just in bareboat charterparties which are the subject of the Diablo case, but also in time and even voyage charterparties; in many of these commonly used charterparty forms, we will use a variant of a lien clause allowing lien over hire, freight, sub-freights or sub-hire.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Parties all over the world enter into charterparties on an everyday basis.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore is, of course, a major maritime hub in the world with many shipping businesses setting up companies, subsidiaries and operations in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Besides being impractical, it is inconvenient and the legal fees for registration are unnecessary expenses for businesses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Notwithstanding the recent judicial pronouncements of there being a need to register a charge under section 131(3)(f) or (g), the reality is that the practice of registering was never part of our commercial landscape in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is notable that the Court of Appeal made comparisons with the corresponding laws in the United Kingdom (UK) and Hong Kong, respectively.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would suggest that the comparisons with the UK and Hong Kong are not merely of jurisprudential significance.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whether as admiralty jurisdictions, legal or maritime centres, England and Hong Kong are arguably two of Singapore's closest rivals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While it may be a slight exaggeration to say that maintaining the status quo will put Singapore in a distinct disadvantage compared to Hong Kong, it is important that we continue to make our maritime and legal hub as competitive as possible and minimise or avoid any unnecessary shortfalls that make us less sensitive to the views and needs of the business community.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The proposed amendments under this amendment Bill are also timely in that Singapore is also aiming to be one of the leading international debt restructuring centres in Asia, especially with the amendments to the Companies Act provisions brought in May 2017 with the introduction of the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL) Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In recent years, insolvency cases involving internationally well-known companies have been started or filed in our Courts for various reasons, such as insolvency protection and debt restructuring.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They include companies in shipping or oil and offshore industries, too.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The proposed amendments will bring about some certainty to the interpretation of section 131(f) and 131(g) of the Companies Act, while the amendments themselves will not necessarily put any party in a position of great disadvantage.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As the law currently stands, given the Court of Appeal and High Court decisions that characterise a lien on sub-freight as a floating charge and a charge on the company's book debts, a shipowner must register its lien as a charge under the Companies Act, failing which, this lien will not be valid against other creditors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this requirement is viewed by the industry as onerous and commercially inconvenient for charterparties that are usually of relatively short durations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This reform would resolve the dilemma shipowners face between expediency and protection of their right to exercise the lien.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The proposed statutory carve out differs from the Hong Kong approach, which the Minister has also mentioned, which provides under section 334(4) of its Companies Ordinance that a lien on sub-freights is not a charge on book debts of the company or a floating charge for the purposes of registration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that the outcome on the registration requirements is, in effect, the same, can the Minister clarify if there are any other practical implications that are intended in affirming the Singapore Courts' characterisation of a lien on sub-freight as a charge on book debts of the company or a floating charge?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given the lack of clarity on the characterisation and registration requirements of liens on sub-freights prior to the Courts' decisions and this amendment, shipping companies and creditors would understandably have acted according to what is most commercially expedient.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In practice, registration of liens on sub-freights is not commonplace, especially for shorter charters.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify whether these penal consequences will be applied against shipping companies and their officers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Clarifications notwithstanding, I stand in support of this Bill, which provides much needed clarity on this area of law and is in line with commercial practice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In their speeches, they have highlighted the practical difficulties that would be faced by shipping companies if the requirements for a lien to be registered were maintained.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The difficulties that they have described are very real.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For that reason, it was in response to feedback from the shipping industry, the Singapore Chamber of Maritime Arbitration (SCMA), and also looking at the Court decision, that we move very quickly to put forward these amendments to Parliament.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first was, he asked, given the approach of Singapore and Hong Kong gives the same practical outcome, whether there were practical implications or differences between the two.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the practical implication of affirming the Court's characterisation of the lien as a charge, as I explained earlier in my speech, this results in Shipowner's Liens retaining their nature as security.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This affords enhanced protection to shipowners and charterers in the event of default and insolvency, as they will be secured creditors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Otherwise, the shipowners and charterers would have to compete with unsecured creditors for payment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In short, with these amendments, in Singapore, a lien is still a charge and, because it is a charge, it will rank ahead of charges which are created after it, and it will also rank ahead of unsecured claims.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In Hong Kong, it is not a security at all and does not have to be registered.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in Hong Kong, the lien will rank together with unsecured claims after secured creditors and, as Mr Dennis Tan pointed out, this, in fact, puts us in a better position.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With respect to Mr Louis Ng's second question on whether, because until the new amendments take effect, he said the lienor company and officers may be guilty of an offence, and asked for clarification on whether there will be penal consequences against the shipping companies and their officers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First and foremost, I should clarify, it is not the case that all Shipowner's Liens created prior to the effective date of these amendments need to be registered.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They will only be regarded as having been registrable in the event of winding up or other creditor acquiring an interest.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, unless this has already occurred, you would not know at this stage whether those Liens are registrable or not, as these are contingent events.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Compared to the overall number of Shipowners' Liens, we would expect that the number affected by winding up or other creditors acquiring an interest, and hence being registrable, to be a small proportion of the whole.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In those instances, suffice to say that this will be a matter for prosecutorial discretion.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In exercising that discretion, the Registrar of Companies will take a practical and commercial approach and all relevant factors, including the fact that current industry practice is not to register and the fact that it was an open question of whether such Liens were registrable until the Diablo case was decided.
